beats.role_note: COLD OPEN LAW — composer, ask lands answered. Speaks the author's name.
beats.narration_text: I'm Uday Sonawane. Two papers, on the same literature, with titles that are almost exact opposites. One says most claimed findings in financial economics are likely false. The other says most claimed findings in return predictability are likely true. They are both serious, and the thing they disagree about is not the data.
beats.new_visual_element: Claude composer, the topic question, answered

shot.show: the Claude composer with the topic question and its three-line answer

props.command: claude "can you trust a published trading signal? two papers, opposite conclusions — why?"
props.segment: Uday Sonawane · Likely False, Likely True
output: one says raise the bar to t > 3.0
the other says the false rate is under 9%

beats.role_note: the two titles, side by side — the premise correction for a topic given as a whole field
beats.narration_text: Algorithmic trading is a field, not a claim, so there is nothing in it to check. The decidable question underneath it is this: when a paper reports a signal that predicted returns, should you believe it. And on that, the literature contains two peer-reviewed answers whose titles contradict each other almost word for word. That disagreement is the subject, because resolving it tells you what to ask of any such claim.

shot.show: the two paper titles set against each other
shot.visual_intent: Two bordered cards stacked. The upper, soft ink: the 2016 title with its claim that most findings are likely false. The lower, terracotta: the later title claiming most are likely true. Between them a short connector and the words 'same literature'.

beats.role_note: PROOF rubric — three questions for any claimed predictive edge, AS A STRUCTURE first
beats.narration_text: Three questions for any claimed edge. One: how many things were tried — because the more candidates you test, the higher the best one scores by luck alone. Two: what does false mean here — because a result that fails a significance test is not the same thing as a result that is untrue. Three: whose bar, and why that one — because the threshold is a choice, and moving it moves the headline.
beats.new_visual_element: the three questions, as a numbered structure

shot.show: three numbered cards: HOW MANY WERE TRIED / WHAT DOES FALSE MEAN / WHOSE BAR
shot.visual_intent: Three bordered cards land in a row, one per narration step. The second lands in terracotta — it is where the two papers actually part company — and the rest of the reel is scored against all three.

beats.role_note: the factor zoo, measured, from the paper's own text
beats.narration_text: First, the scale of the problem. The 2016 paper catalogues three hundred and sixteen different factors, drawn from three hundred and thirteen articles, two hundred and fifty of them published. And the rate is accelerating: about one new factor a year in the eighties, around five a year through the nineties and early two-thousands, and roughly eighteen a year in the paper's final nine years. A hundred and sixty-four factors in those nine years alone — roughly double the eighty-four from all previous years put together.
beats.new_visual_element: the catalogue and its growth rate

shot.show: 316 factors from 313 articles, and the per-year discovery rate rising
shot.visual_intent: Left: two stat cards, 316 factors and 313 articles. Right: three ascending bars labelled with the eras and their per-year rates, the last in terracotta. Beneath, one line: 164 in nine years against 84 in all prior years. Citation strip names the paper and journal.

beats.role_note: the multiple-testing argument, and the observation that gives it force
beats.narration_text: Here is the argument. If hundreds of candidates are tested and only the winners get published, then the usual significance bar is far too low, because it was designed for one test and not for hundreds. So the paper proposes raising it: a newly discovered factor should clear a t-ratio above three, not the customary two. And there is one observation that makes this bite — in their sample, the overwhelming majority of published t-statistics clear the old bar. Nearly everything published passes, which tells you about the filter rather than about the world.
beats.new_visual_element: the proposed bar, and the filter observation

shot.show: t > 3.0 against the customary 2.0, and nearly all published results clearing the old bar
shot.visual_intent: Top: two bordered chips, 'the customary bar, t > 2.0' in soft ink and 'what they propose, t > 3.0' in terracotta, with a short gap drawn between them. Beneath, a bordered panel quoting the observation that the overwhelming majority of published t-statistics exceed the old benchmark. Cited.

beats.role_note: the rebuttal — a Federal Reserve Board paper arguing the opposite, with numbers
beats.narration_text: Now the other side, and it is not a blog post. A Federal Reserve Board economist puts bounds on the false discovery rate directly. Using the summary statistics of previous studies, he finds the false rate is at most twenty-five percent in eight of nine of them. A tighter bound puts it at nine percent or below. And for the main specification he reports a bound of eight and a half percent — which is to say at least ninety-one and a half percent of those published findings are true.

shot.show: FDR at most 25% in 8 of 9 studies, a refined bound of 9%, and 8.5% for the main specification
shot.visual_intent: Three descending bordered bars with their percentages: 25% at the top in soft ink, 9% below it, and 8.5% in terracotta at the bottom, each captioned with what it bounds. Beneath, one line: at least 91.5% of those findings are true. Citation strip names the author, institution and arXiv id.

beats.role_note: WHY they disagree — question 2, and it is definitional rather than empirical
beats.narration_text: So which is right. The striking part is that the rebuttal does not dispute the earlier paper's arithmetic. It argues that the earlier paper's own methods imply a false rate of about nine percent, and that the gap comes from what the word false was taken to mean — counting every factor that failed a significance test as a false discovery. Insignificant and untrue are not the same category. A disagreement about a definition had been reading, for a decade, as a disagreement about the facts.

shot.show: insignificant versus untrue, and the same methods yielding 9%
shot.visual_intent: Two bordered cards side by side: 'failed a significance test' in soft ink and 'is not true' in terracotta, with a crossed equals sign drawn BETWEEN them, never through either label. Beneath, a panel noting that the earlier paper's own methods imply a rate of about 9%. Cited.

beats.role_note: what survives the disagreement — the part both sides share
beats.narration_text: What survives is the part neither side contests. Hundreds of candidate signals were tested. Only the ones that worked were written up. Whatever the true false rate turns out to be, the published record is a filtered sample, and the number that would settle it — how many specifications were tried and discarded — is the one number no paper reports. That is why the earlier authors had to estimate it from the size of the literature rather than read it off.
beats.new_visual_element: the shared premise, and the unreported number

shot.show: the filter both sides agree on, and the trial count nobody publishes
shot.visual_intent: A funnel drawn in soft ink: many small candidate marks entering at the top, a narrow neck labelled 'only the winners are written up', and a few marks below. To the right, a terracotta panel: 'the number that would settle it — trials run and discarded — is the one nobody reports'.

beats.role_note: the rubric scored, then the two-sided verdict
beats.narration_text: Scored. How many were tried: three hundred and sixteen published, and an unknown multiple of that discarded. What does false mean: the two papers used different definitions, and that accounts for most of the gap. Whose bar: one proposes three, the field's habit is two, and the rebuttal works at two deliberately. So — be excited that this argument is being had with arithmetic rather than opinion, and that a bound can be put on the false rate at all. Be sceptical of anyone quoting either headline without the definition attached, and of any backtest that does not say how many were run.
beats.new_visual_element: the rubric answered, then the two-sided verdict

shot.show: three rubric rows answered, then BE EXCITED ABOUT / BE SCEPTICAL OF
shot.visual_intent: Three label-and-chip rows score the rubric. Beneath, two lines: BE EXCITED ABOUT in ink, BE SCEPTICAL OF in terracotta.

beats.role_note: scaffolded task — the rubric on the next claimed edge, with GOOD/BAD
beats.narration_text: Your turn. Next time you meet a claimed edge — in a paper, a pitch deck, or your own notebook — ask three things: how many variants were tried before this one, what the author counts as a failure, and what the threshold would have to be before this result stopped being interesting. The first question is usually the one nobody has written down.

shot.show: the composer with the handoff prompt and a GOOD/BAD discriminator

props.command: claude "for this result: how many variants were tried, what counts as a failure here, and at what threshold would it stop being interesting?"
props.segment: Your turn · how many did you try

BAD: a t-stat with no denominator
insignificant is not the same as untrue
